newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU begins bid to paper over cracks in U.S. ties.
newsitem.headline: EU begins bid to paper over cracks in U.S. ties.

text.p: The European Union, committed to improving relations with the United States after a year strained by trade disputes, begins a campaign to paper over the cracks with a high-level visit to Washington on Tuesday.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan are to hold talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.

They are also to meet Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Stuart Eizenstat, Undersecretary of State for economic affairs and also the special envoy appointed to explain Washington's controversial Helms-Burton Act to the world.

The act, which amalgamates decades of Washington's anti-Cuba policy, was chiefly responsible for putting strain on the world's largest trade partnership and still remains a bitter transatlantic divide.

Named for its congressional sponsors, the act allows among other things for naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreign companies or individuals deemed to have profited from investments in property confiscated by the Cuban government since the communist revolution of 1959.

This part has now twice been suspended for six months -- the last time on January 3 -- but a bitter wrangle is still to be played out at the World Trade Organisation in Geneva where the EU has lodged a formal complaint.

Tuesday's visit, while unlikely to ignore these differences, will instead try to focus on the positive, including discussing progresss on mutual recognition agreements (MRAs), common ground on international technology agreements, and the ongoing global telecommunications trade talks in Geneva.
On foreign policy matters, the EU delegation will discuss the Middle East, former Yugoslavia, the African Great Lakes region and Turkish/Greek disputes over Cyprus.
"It's a lot to get through in one day," said a European Commission spokesman, "but this really is a first opportunity to meet the people who will make up the new U.S. administration."

The visit will chiefly lay the groundwork for the next EU/U.S. summit to be held in the Netherlands sometime in May as part of the much-vaunted New Transatlantic Agenda, the formal name given to relations between Washington and Europe.

Launched in December 1995, the agenda sought ways of involving business and industry in government decision-making and has already been praised by some business chiefs as having cut through much red tape.

One group established under the scheme, the Transatlantic Business Dialogue, is moving towards finalising MRAs so that imports and exports between the two partners need no longer undergo costly and time-consuming secondary certification procedures.

"This is very much a getting-to-know-you sort of meeting," said a Commission official. "But the U.S. is our strongest and most important trade and foreign policy ally and so even the most fleeting meetings are often crucial to the relationship."
